plan.concept: RANSAC robustly fits a model to noisy data containing outliers by iteratively generating hypotheses from minimal random samples and counting supporting inliers.
learningObjectives: Explain how RANSAC uses a minimal sample set (two points for a line) to construct a candidate model
Identify how the inlier threshold separates consensus points from outliers
Describe how RANSAC evaluates multiple random hypotheses to find the model with the highest consensus
plan.keyInsight: Instead of trying to fit all noisy points at once, RANSAC finds the correct model by generating random guesses and choosing the one that gets the most 'votes' (inliers) from the rest of the dataset.

interactions.label: RANSAC Iteration
interactions.effect: Changes the two randomly sampled points (highlighted in red) and the resulting candidate line, updating which other points are detected as inliers (blue).
interactions.teaches: Shows how different random samples yield different model hypotheses, some poor (low inliers) and some excellent (high inliers).

interactions.label: Inlier Threshold
interactions.effect: Visualizes the tolerance band (shaded region) around the candidate line, changing which points fall close enough to be marked as inliers.
interactions.teaches: Demonstrates how the distance threshold defines what counts as 'consensus', balancing strictness against noise tolerance.

demo_steps.title: Forming a Hypothesis
demo_steps.narration: Welcome to RANSAC! Look at the red line: it is a candidate model generated by randomly picking just two points (highlighted in red). Because this iteration randomly picked points from a flat outlier cluster, the resulting horizontal line represents a poor fit for the overall diagonal trend of the dataset.
demo_steps.focus: The two red points on the horizontal line, indicating the minimal sample used to define this model.

demo_steps.title: Counting the Consensus
demo_steps.narration: To evaluate this candidate model, we count how many other points support it. With our current threshold, only two additional points (highlighted in blue) fall close enough to the line, giving us a total of 4 inliers. The white points are ignored as outliers for this hypothesis.
demo_steps.focus: The blue inlier points and the surrounding white outlier points.

demo_steps.title: Adjusting Tolerance
demo_steps.narration: Try widening the tolerance threshold. Notice how the shaded region around the line expands, and more points turn blue. If the threshold is too large, we risk falsely accepting clear outliers as inliers; if it is too small, we might reject valid data due to minor noise.
demo_steps.focus: The expanding shaded tolerance band and the newly recruited blue inliers.

demo_steps.title: Finding the True Trend
demo_steps.narration: Let's move to a different iteration. Here, RANSAC randomly picked two points that actually lie along the main diagonal trend. Even with a narrow threshold, look at how many points now fall inside the consensus corridor! This high inlier count tells RANSAC that this candidate line is a much better fit.
demo_steps.focus: The diagonal red line and the large cluster of blue inliers supporting it.

plan.reconstructionNotes: An interactive 2D scatter plot representing the line-fitting RANSAC example. It contains about 12 points: a dominant diagonal line trend with some noise, and a horizontal cluster of outlier points on the upper right. When iteration=1, the candidate line is horizontal, passing through two red points; two nearby points are blue (inliers), and the rest are white. A shaded band represents the threshold area. When iteration=2, the candidate line is diagonal, passing through two diagonal red points, with most of the diagonal points turning blue. The user can adjust the threshold slider to visually expand/contract the shaded corridor around the active line, dynamically changing point colors between blue (inlier) and white (outlier).
